blk_part_01_part_1_a_greeting_measures_t.text: What about handshakes and hugs? In some English-speaking countries, such as Australia and New Zealand, cheek kisses happen only among close friends, and handshakes or hugs are more common greetings. A handshake or a hug can do the same job as a kiss: it says how close two people are, but with a different kind of touch.

We let a person into a closer zone when we feel closer to them. Americans like about the same personal space as people in northern and central Europe. In Japan, everyday greetings usually have less touching, so kisses, hugs and handshakes are less common than in many other places.

blk_part_04_part_4_why_american_workers_.text: History helps explain this. In 1919, Prohibition put money pressure on restaurants in the USA. So they accepted tips to add to their workers' pay. blk_part_04_part_4_why_american_workers_.text: But the system has problems. Tipping can feel awkward, because people are not sure how much to give. It is also not always fair. People sometimes tip by the price of the meal, not by the quality of the service. And the system is hard to change. Some people argue that changing the tip rules could favor servers who get tips over staff who do not get tips, and make income less equal.

blk_part_05_part_5_what_a_meal_protects.text: In France, enjoying food is an important value. In the 20th century, Georges Auguste Escoffier wrote down the rules of high French cooking. Today, a lunch break usually lasts at least one hour. Eating lunch at your desk is even illegal. But a long lunch does not mean a big meal. On busy workdays in Paris, lunches with many courses are not common. French food has also changed. Many modern meals are simpler, and some dishes come from immigrant cooking. Fast food and new habits among young people put pressure on the old food culture. Even so, France works to keep it, for example through education programs in schools.
